accuracy.evidence: Checked against the DfE 2013 national curriculum for England, Year 1 handwriting (statutory: form lower-case letters in the correct direction, starting and finishing in the right place; understand which letters belong to which handwriting 'families' and practise these). The four families (long ladder l i t u; curly caterpillar c a d g o q; one-armed robot r n m h b; zigzag v w z) match the groupings used by common UK schemes, and the adult text says that some schemes move e, s, f, k and p, so parents match their school. Every start dot in the lab is the first point of the letter's first stroke: top of the ascender for l, h, b, d's c start just below the middle line on the right, the middle line for n, r, t's top. Anticlockwise curl for c-family letters matches every UK scheme checked.

misconceptions.evidence: Targets the handwriting slips teachers report most: starting at the bottom (step 1 prediction 'At the bottom', step 5 l and t drawn from the bottom, challenge 'bottom'); going round o, a and d clockwise (step 2 rejects a clockwise curl with 'Wrong way round', step 5 o and d reversed, challenge 'clock'); starting d or a with the stick (step 1 decoy dot 3 on d and a, feedback 'd does not start with its stick'); sorting by height (step 3 prediction about d, h feedback 'h is tall, but h goes down, back up and over: a robot letter', challenge 'tall'); and stopping a robot letter after the down stroke (step 2 'Keep going. n is a robot letter: down, back up the line, then over').

lab_distinct.evidence: flagltrfam is built on this topic's own mechanism: a hand-drawn stroke model of 20 small letters on four writing lines, start-dot hunting on the real first point of each stroke, a gesture classifier that tells a straight pull, an anticlockwise curl, a clockwise curl, a down-up-over and a zigzag apart by the turning of the drag, family sorting by first move, and reversed-stroke slips. flagcaps (capital letters) traces capitals with no family idea; flagjoin teaches joins; flaggrip is pencil grip. lab_distinct passed under 30% against every flagship lab.

lab_teaches.evidence: The learner finds the rule by doing: tapping the end of l returns 'That is where l finishes. Start at the other end: pull down from the top'; a clockwise drag on o returns 'Wrong way round. o is a curly c letter: curl back over the top, to the left'; sorting d into ladder returns 'd starts like c, so it is a curly c letter'. Each correct start makes the letter grow stroke by stroke from that dot, and the done screens list the four first moves.

predictions.evidence: Two predictions with tempting wrong answers: 'Where does the pencil start on most small letters?' (At the bottom is disproved by six letters that all start at the top of their first shape) and 'd has a tall stick, like l. Which family is d in?' (ladder, like l is disproved when d, a and g land in curly c and the done message says the first move decides the family, not the height).

challenge_feedback.evidence: Six challenge questions; every wrong option has its own message naming the slip: 'ladder' (ladder letters only pull straight down), 'robot' (down, back up and over), 'bottom' (small letters never start at the bottom), 'middle' (l starts at the very top line), 'clock' (o curls back over the top, to the left, like c), 'tall' (being tall does not choose the family), 'curl' (h starts with a long pull down) and 'abc' (families are about the first move, not the ABC).

readability.evidence: Kid text measured FK grade 1.6 against the family limit of 5.0: short sentences such as 'Start like c. Curl back over the top, to the left.' Adult text measured within the 10.0 limit after the curriculum paragraph was split into short sentences. Canvas instructions are one line each ('Letter 1 of 6: tap where the pencil starts', 'Green dot: the start. Arrow: the way it goes.') and the family names are single words a 5-year-old hears in class.

no_filler.evidence: Every kid sentence gives a rule or a family with its letters; the adult text gives the Year 1 requirement, the scheme names and variations, why families help (one move, later joins), five named mistakes and what each lab step does. The content gate found no filler phrases and the explanation is under 12% the same as Forming Capital Letters, Joining Letters and every other lesson.

mobile.evidence: Checked on 360 px Android screenshots in light and dark themes for all six steps: the letter card is about 230 px wide with 34 px start dots, the four family boxes sit side by side at about 80 px each with the sorted letters drawn two per row, the sort card was shrunk to 70 by 80 px after the first screenshot showed its hint touching the boxes, and the odd-one-out row of four 80 px letter cards fits without clipping. The walkthrough passed on iPhone 13.

accessibility.evidence: Every canvas action has a button below it: Dot 1 to 3 (aria-label names the letter and the numbered dot drawn on the canvas, e.g. 'Start l at dot 1'), the four first moves by name, the four family names, one button per letter in the odd-one-out row, and the three slip choices. The canvas aria-label is updated after every action, the challenge feedback is a role=status live region, and axe (WCAG 2.1 AA) found no violations in either theme on desktop and iPhone 13.
